title: The unsent letter
hookLine: write it all, then don't send it

lines: A MESSAGE IN THE Versions FOLDER.
UNFAIR IN PLACES, RIGHT IN OTHERS.
cards: There's a message sitting in a versions folder. It's been there for months. It's long, unfair in places and exactly right in others.
It says everything that never got said at the funeral, or in the breakup, or at the last family dinner. Every so often its writer opens it, adds a line, and closes it again.
It has never been sent, and that may be the wisest thing about it. Today: the unsent letter.

teach.b: First, the old permission to pour it all out. Psalm 62 says: "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him." Pour, not a measured spoonful, not the polite version.
The psalms hold a great deal of speech that goes up and gets no reply on the page: grief, rage, pleading, thanks. The letter is a little like that. It gets to be whole.

teach.h: COMMUNE WITH YOUR HEART, BE STILL.
teach.b: Psalm 4 says: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." Talk it through with yourself, then stop. An unsent letter does both: you write until there's nothing left to say, then put the pen down.
Third, why not send it. Yesterday's limit applies: repair that would injure someone isn't repair, and a letter written in full heat often would.

The unsent letter keeps the honesty and drops the damage. Some counselors suggest it for that reason, and for the dead, the unreachable, or the person it isn't safe to contact. Fourth, what to do with it.

teach.h: IN A DRAWER, OR IN THE FIRE.
teach.b: Keep it in a drawer and read it in a month, noticing what's changed.
Some people burn it or tear it up as a small ending. The point isn't the paper. The words left your head and went somewhere, so you don't have to keep rehearsing them in the car.

how: Some counselors and grief groups suggest writing a letter to a person who hurt you, or who has died, and keeping it rather than sending it; Jews and Christians who pray the psalms often describe them as a place to pour out what can't be said elsewhere.

o: a letter saved to send later, once you've calmed down
an email that failed to send and got stuck there

games.q: you've written the long letter. every word of it is true, and some of it is cruel. what do you do with it?
o: send it tonight, while it's fresh.
keep it, and read it again in a month.
post it where they'll see it.
games.why: the practice keeps it. said, not sent: the words leave your head without landing on anyone.

practice: With a pen, or a blank note on your phone with no recipient, write one person's name at the top, then write fast, without fixing anything: what happened, what it cost you, what you wish they knew.
Don't be fair or polite; nobody will read it. When it's emptied out, add one last line, I've said it, and put the page somewhere safe. If you pray, you can offer it up, poured out, as the psalm says.

wordCard.voice: Versions folder. Where an honest letter can sit, written all the way down to someone, and never delivered. Today's word.
